summary: This Wikipedia-derived note surveys the effects of economic inequality on health, social outcomes, growth, poverty and development. It covers Wilkinson and Pickett's cross-country and US-state comparisons, the gender pay gap, life expectancy, and the mixed research on whether inequality helps or hinders economic growth, including Barro, Perotti, Galor and Zeira, and Piketty's critique of the Kuznets curve. It closes with the link between inequality and poverty reduction and a quote from UN Secretary General Ban Ki-Moon.
one_line: Overview of economic inequality's effects on health, social problems, economic growth, property rights and poverty reduction, with competing research findings.
key_facts: Richard G. Wilkinson and Kate Pickett found higher rates of health and social problems in countries and states with higher inequality, using statistics from 23 developed countries and the 50 US states.
Japan and Finland were cited as countries with high equality and lower social and health problems, while the US and UK had large differences in household income.
The income gap in other countries ranges from 53% in Botswana to -40% in Bahrain, according to the note's gender pay gap discussion.
Americans lived about 77 years on average in 2004, compared with 78 years for Greeks and 78 for New Zealanders, though the USA has a higher GDP per capita.
Life expectancy in Sweden (80 years) and Japan (82) was longer, in countries where income was more equally distributed.
Harvard economist Robert Barro found "little overall relation between income inequality and rates of growth and investment".
According to work by Barro in 1999 and 2000, high levels of inequality reduce growth in relatively poor countries but encourage growth in richer countries.
An IMF study found a strong association between lower levels of inequality in developing countries and sustained periods of economic growth.
In 1993, Galor and Zeira showed that inequality in the presence of credit market imperfections has a long lasting detrimental effect on human capital formation and economic development.
A 1996 study by Perotti concluded that "more equal societies have lower fertility rates and higher rates of investment in education."
In some countries it can take over 200 steps and up to 14 years to build on government land, a bureaucratic cause of extra-legal property ownership.
2013 Economics Nobel prize winner Robert J. Shiller said that rising inequality in the United States and elsewhere is the most important problem.

Thomas Piketty claims that from 1914 to 1945 wars and "violent economic and political shocks" reduced inequality and that the Kuznets curve cannot account for rising inequality in the developed world since the 1970s.
For a country with low inequality, a growth rate of 2% per head and 40% of the population in poverty can halve poverty in ten years, while a high-inequality country would take nearly 60 years.
Ban Ki-Moon, Secretary General of the United Nations, said: "While economic growth is necessary, it is not sufficient for progress on reducing poverty."
